n: In this lecture we give an introduction to forensic traumatology. The word traumatology comes from the Greek trauma, meaning injury, and logos, meaning study; it is the science of injuries. In clinical medicine it is concerned mainly with identifying injuries, that is, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, that is, prophylaxis. Forensic traumatology, by contrast, establishes the mechanism and time of injury and the object that caused it, and gives a forensic medical assessment of the injury.

The concept of bodily injury is defined differently in law and in forensic medicine. In criminal law, bodily injury is harm to health caused by unlawful acts committed intentionally or through negligence. In forensic medicine, bodily injury is a disruption of the anatomical integrity or physiological function of organs and tissues as a result of external action. Such a disruption may lead to deterioration of health or to death. Attention, there is a risk of error: bodily injury is not a disease. If the same disruption is due to an internal cause, it is called a disease.

Four types of injuring external action are distinguished: physical, chemical, biological and mental. Physical factors include mechanical, thermal, electrical, barometric and radiation action. Chemical factors are poisons, chemicals and medicines. Biological factors are plant and animal toxins and microorganisms. The mental factor is strong emotion and fear. The consequences of mental action are usually studied by forensic psychiatry; a forensic psychiatric examination is then ordered. Sometimes the combined action of several external factors may also be observed.

Physical action is divided into five types: mechanical, thermal, barometric, electrical and radiation. Mechanical action includes blunt and sharp objects, firearms and explosives. Thermal action is high and low temperature. Barometric action is raised and lowered atmospheric pressure. Electrical action is technical and atmospheric electric current. Radiation action is X-rays and isotopes. Several factors may act together. Attention: mental action is not physical; it is studied by forensic psychiatry.

t: Forms of factor: object, substance, phenomenon
n: An injuring factor may take the form of an object, a substance or a state, that is, a phenomenon. Objects have a stable shape with constant dimensions. Attention: an object is not a substance, because substances do not have a stable shape. Substances occur in three states: solid, for example sand and soil; liquid, for example acid and alkali; gaseous, for example carbon monoxide and methane. States or phenomena include electric current and changes in pressure.

In classifying trauma, the type of action, the region of injury and the number of injuries, that is, single or multiple, are taken into account. By type of action, simple trauma results from a single factor, and combined trauma from two or more types. By region, a limited injury lies in one region or segment, and a dual injury in two or more regions. Example: a stab wound of the chest is a simple limited single injury. A rib fracture and a thermal burn are a complex dual multiple injury. Remember: the concepts of simple and complex trauma are not identical.

t: Limited and dual, single and multiple injuries
n: If an injury occupies one anatomical region or one segment of the musculoskeletal system, it is called limited. If two or more regions or segments are injured, it is a dual injury. By number, single and multiple injuries are distinguished. Examples: a stab wound of the chest is one factor, simple limited single. Concussion and abdominal bruising are one factor, simple dual multiple. A rib fracture and a thermal burn are a mechanical and a thermal factor, complex dual multiple. Attention: simple or complex depends on the number of factors, and limited or dual on the number of regions. They are not the same concept.

In forensic medical examination, especially of corpses and living persons, mechanical injuries occupy the leading place. In recent years, mechanical injuries rank after cardiovascular and oncological diseases among causes of death. Injuries are divided into anatomical and functional groups. The predominantly anatomical group includes abrasion, bruise, wound, fracture, dislocation, crushing and rupture of internal organs. The predominantly functional group includes shock from a blow to a reflexogenic zone, concussion of the brain and internal organs, and aspiration asphyxia.

Now let us consider a case analysis. Case 1: a stab wound of the chest has been found. In the source this is classified as a simple limited single injury. Case 2: there is concussion of the brain and bruises in the abdominal region. The source calls this a simple dual multiple injury. Case 3: a rib fracture and a thermal burn occur together. The source assesses this as a complex dual multiple injury. Question: classify each case, justifying it by the number of factors, the number of regions and the number of injuries.

t: The concept of traumatism and its types
n: Traumatism is the totality of similar injuries occurring in a group of persons under the same working and living conditions. The types of traumatism are mainly linked to the nature of persons' activities. Occupational traumatism includes industry, agriculture and construction. Transport traumatism covers road, motorcycle, bicycle, railway, air and water transport. Military traumatism is divided into wartime and peacetime. Other types: street, sports, school and domestic traumatism. Occupational, transport and military traumatism are further divided into internal varieties.

Most injuries arise from failure to comply with established rules and procedures. This includes the consumption of alcohol, narcotics and other intoxicating substances. In recent times injuries have been increasing in all countries of the world, and among them the share of complex injuries is growing. On the basis of forensic medical examination materials, the factors that caused the injury are studied and concrete proposals and recommendations for prevention are given.

t: Quick question and case analysis: traumatism
n: Now a quick question. A worker was injured on a construction site. Which type of traumatism is this, and which internal variety? Case analysis: a motorcyclist was injured on the street through breaking the rules. Which type does this belong to, and which factor is significant? Answer: the first is occupational traumatism, construction. The second is transport traumatism, motorcycle, the cause being non-compliance with the rules. Attention: traumatism is not an individual injury but the totality of similar injuries. Do not confuse it with a single bodily injury.

t: Determining the vitality of injuries: significance
n: Determining the vitality of an injury is extremely important in forensic medical examination, because an injury may also be inflicted after a person's death. This may be done deliberately: dismemberment of the corpse or alteration of the original scene relating to the cause of death. It may also be inflicted accidentally: during resuscitation, examination and transport of the corpse, and also by animals, birds and fish. Vitality is established by signs of the reaction of the organism, organ or tissue to the injury. In practice changes in the circulatory system are chiefly important.

Let us list the general signs of vitality. External and internal bleeding and general anaemia of the internal organs indicate vitality. In the airways, aspiration of blood and foreign matter is observed. In the stomach and intestine, blood and foreign matter are found, and in injured organs small fragments. Myoglobin is present in the urine and renal tubules. When areas with fatty tissue are injured, erythrocytes and fat are found in the lymph. Regional lymph nodes contain erythrocytes; this is erythrophagia. Air, fat, tissue or foreign-matter emboli are also identified.

Local signs are found in the area of the injury itself and confirm the vitality of the injury. They fall into several groups: haemorrhage and thrombus in a vessel; reactive oedema and signs of inflammation; muscle contraction and cell necrosis; and histochemical changes. The distinctness of the signs depends on the type, number and extent of the injuries and on the features of the organism and region. Attention: in phylogenetically ancient tissues a post-mortem injury may resemble a vital one.

t: Case analysis: the question of vitality
n: Let us analyse the following situation. An injury has been found on a corpse; was it inflicted during life or after death? After death an injury may be inflicted deliberately or accidentally. The distinctness of the signs of vitality depends on the type, number and extent of the injury, and on the features of the organism and of the injured region. In phylogenetically older tissues, vital processes cease slowly after death, so a post-mortem injury may resemble a vital one. Attention: a post-mortem injury is not a vital injury. Question: why may it be mistaken to judge an injury as vital by its outward appearance alone?

Bodily injuries are first examined macroscopically. In all cases the appropriate measurements are made: the type, site, shape and size of the injury and distances are determined. The distance of the injury from a certain region of the body is also measured; this is important in car accident trauma, suicide and homicide. Radiography reveals a foreign body and bone injury. Colour prints and spectral methods show metal particles and traces. The histological method establishes vitality and age of injury. Stereomicroscopy is used for three-dimensional study, and traceological examination to identify the injuring object.

When medical help is sought, it is important for clinicians to study injuries in the same way and to describe them fully in the medical records. After some time these records are placed at the disposal of the forensic medical examination that has been ordered. Superficial study of the injury, an incomplete description, or limiting oneself to a diagnosis alone creates serious difficulty in carrying out the tasks of the examination. In some cases, forensic biological, forensic chemical, histochemical and other laboratory methods are used to resolve the questions.

t: Mechanical injuries: basic condition and classification
n: The basic condition of mechanical injuries is movement: the injuring object or the body must be in motion. Its property depends on kinetic energy. The extent of injury is directly proportional to mass and velocity. By classification, a blunt object, a sharp object and a firearm are distinguished. Attention: a weapon, an implement and an object are not the same. A weapon is made for attack or defence, for example a pistol, rifle or dagger. An implement is used in industry and the household, for example an axe, saw or scissors. An object has no definite purpose, for example a stone or a stick.

t: Factors on which the type of mechanical injury depends
n: The type and extent of a mechanical injury depend on three things: the injuring agent, the region injured, and their interaction. On the side of the agent, the mass of the object, hardness, velocity, and properties of the injuring surface or of the point and blade are important. On the side of the region, anatomical and physiological features, the person's age and the presence of disease are important. The number and duration of interactions are also important. Sometimes environmental conditions are also taken into account.

t: Death from mechanical injury: primary causes
n: Let us consider the primary causes of death from mechanical injury. A primary cause leads to death at the time of injury or within a short time. This includes an injury incompatible with life: severing of the head, division of the body in two, crushing of the head. Such injuries occur mainly in transport trauma, falls from a great height and explosions. Contusion of vital organs, that is, the brain and heart, is also a primary cause; cardiac concussion leads to reflex arrest. A secondary cause develops after some time, for example an infectious complication: sepsis, tetanus.

In blood loss, not only the volume of blood lost but also the rate of loss is important. In acute blood loss a large artery is injured, and even with a loss of up to 500 ml death occurs in the first minutes. The brain and heart are anaemic, the spleen is dark, and the cadaveric lividity is usual. In massive blood loss, more than 50%, that is, 2.5 l or more, is lost; the process lasts several hours, the spleen is contracted, and cadaveric lividity is late and less marked. Minakov spots are ribbon-like haemorrhages beneath the endocardium of the left ventricle of the heart; a sign of acute blood loss. Attention: in massive blood loss they are found only in some cases.

t: Traumatic shock and compression of organs
n: Traumatic shock is a serious disturbance of the function of the central nervous, cardiovascular and endocrine systems; peripheral circulation is insufficient. Usually severe grade III-IV shock leads to death. Venous plethora, pooling of blood in the liver and spleen, and impaired microcirculation may be found. In craniocerebral injury, epidural, subdural and subarachnoid haematomas compress the brain, and in injury of the cervicothoracic spine, the spinal cord. In injury of the chest wall, haemopericardium, pneumothorax and haemothorax arise and may compress the heart and lungs.

t: Air embolism and the Sunsov test
n: Air embolism may develop in injury of large veins and in criminal abortion. 5-7 cubic cm of air dissolves slowly; if 10 cubic cm or more enters quickly, there is a danger of death. The Sunsov test is carried out step by step. One begins with the chest, the sternum is separated, water is poured into the pericardium, and the wall of the right ventricle is punctured. The escape of air bubbles through the water is considered a positive result.

Fat embolism is observed mainly in fractures of long tubular bones and in crushing of the subcutaneous fat layer. Small fat particles accumulate in the pulmonary vessels and gradually close the lumen. For this reason death occurs not immediately but after about 2-3 days. For diagnosis, frozen sections of the lungs and brain are stained. Sudan III shows fat orange-red, and Sudan IV black. In aspiration asphyxia, by contrast, blood enters the airways when the larynx or airways are injured, or in fracture of the base of the skull or nasal bones. On the corpse, blood is found in the airways.

Secondary causes are infectious complications: purulent peritonitis leading to sepsis, pleurisy, meningitis, osteomyelitis, gas gangrene and tetanus. Also intoxication, that is, traumatic toxicosis. Sometimes secondary blood loss, shock, embolism or a malignant tumour at the injury site develops later. Now a case analysis. A large artery has been injured, with blood loss of up to 500 ml. Death occurred in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation of the heart. On the corpse there is anaemia of the brain and heart muscle, while the spleen is full of blood; beneath the endocardium of the left ventricle there are Minakov spots. Question: which cause is this? In massive blood loss, Minakov spots are found only in some cases.

An object that inflicts injury by the action of a certain surface is considered blunt. It may be hard, for example a stone or a stick; soft, for example a scarf or towel; or elastic, for example a rubber ball. If the injury is at the site where the object acted, it is called a direct injury. If it forms in a region other than the site of action, it is an indirect injury. If the object's contact surface is smaller than the surface of the injured region, the surface is limited; if larger, it is unlimited, a broad surface. Attention: this division is relative. One object may have a limited surface in one position and an unlimited one in another.

Depending on the mass of the injuring object and the force of action, the type of trauma is impression or inertial. In impression trauma, the mass of the object is less than the mass of the region, the injury forms only in the area of action, and the damage is limited to that area. In inertial trauma, by contrast, the force is greater than the mass of the region, that is, of the body. Here indirect injuries also form, the body is shaken and a contrecoup occurs. Attention: indirect injury and contrecoup are characteristic of inertial trauma. Impression and inertial trauma are not the same.

t: Mechanisms of action of blunt objects
n: The main mechanisms of action of blunt objects: blow, compression, tension, friction; sometimes twisting and concussion are also observed. A blow is a brief action directed to one side; concussion usually arises after a blow or when the body is shaken. In compression, centripetal forces act, and internal organs and bones are seriously injured. In tension, centrifugal forces produce a lacerated wound, rupture and avulsion. Friction is movement at an angle and forms only a direct abrasion. In twisting, a spiral fracture of the bone occurs. Often two or more mechanisms act together.

An abrasion is a breach of the integrity of the epidermis and the papillary layer: superficial or deep. Forensic medical significance: establishing the mechanical action, the mechanism and age, and sometimes the circumstances of the incident. The stages of abrasion according to Taikov are as follows: fresh abrasion up to 12 hours, crust 2-3 days, epithelialisation 7-9 days, disappearance of the mark 10-15 days. Remember: the time limits are approximate; they depend on age, health, skin features and depth of injury.

An abrasion is a breach of the integrity of the epidermis and the papillary layer: superficial if only the epidermis is damaged, and deep if it reaches the papillary layer. An abrasion forms when a blunt object acts at an angle, by the mechanisms of blow, compression and friction. A linear abrasion is called a scratch. Forensic medical significance: it confirms mechanical action, helps establish the mechanism and age, and sometimes allows the circumstances of the incident to be surmised. Attention: an abrasion is not a parchment spot. A parchment spot is a sign of post-mortem drying: yellowish-brown, with no crust forming. It has no signs of a vital injury; it lies level with the surrounding skin or lower.

A bruise is an effusion of blood into the tissues when a vessel ruptures; accumulation of blood in a cavity is a haematoma. On an unlimited surface the bruise is round or oval, and on a limited surface it reproduces the shape of the object. Colour change begins at the edges; the time limits are approximate and depend on the object and region. In the first days the colour is reddish-bluish and cyanotic; this is the reduction of oxyhaemoglobin. On days 3-4 a green tinge appears, due to verdohaemochromogen and biliverdin. On days 6-8 a yellow tinge, due to bilirubin and haemosiderin. On the eyes, the mucosa of the lips and the neck, however, the reddish-cyanotic colour then fades without turning into different colours.

A wound is a separation of all layers of the skin and deep soft tissues: in a superficial wound only the skin is damaged, and in a deep wound the soft tissues too. Depending on the mechanism, wounds differ: a contused wound results from blow and compression, a crushed wound from strong blow and compression, a lacerated wound from blow and tension, and a flap wound from a blow at an acute angle and tension. The edges are uneven, abraded and haemorrhagic; the ends are usually blunt. The walls and floor are uneven, with tissue "bridges" between the walls. External bleeding is usually not heavy. If no help is given, the wound heals by secondary intention, leaving a coarse scar.

t: Wound shape and identifying the object
n: The shape of a wound depends mainly on the properties of the injuring surface; from it, the object that caused the injury is identified. On an unlimited flat surface, a branching, zigzag or stellate wound forms. A limited flat surface acting perpendicularly gives a three-, four- or multi-rayed stellate wound. On a spherical surface a stellate wound with equal rays forms, with a depressed centre. On a cylindrical surface a slit-like, linear wound forms, with abraded edges. A bite wound is two half-rings: an incisor leaves an elongated mark, a canine a ring-shaped one, a molar a quadrangular one. Attention: a rupture is not a wound. A rupture is indirect; the ends are sharp, the edges smooth, without abrasion.

t: Bone deformation and types of fracture
n: Under external mechanical action, the shape of a bone changes. In temporary deformation the shape is restored after the action ceases; in permanent deformation a fracture forms. In a complete fracture, the two new surfaces allow movement in several directions. In an incomplete fracture, that is, a crack or greenstick fracture, only in one direction. In an open fracture, the injured area of the bone is in direct communication with the external environment; in a closed fracture there is no such communication. The shape of the fracture may be linear, broken, perforated, comminuted or depressed. The direction of the line is transverse, longitudinal, diagonal, annular or spiral.

In bending, compression arises on the side of the action and tension on the opposite side. Bone is less resistant to tension, so a fracture begins first on the tension side. On the tension side, the fracture line is single, straight and transverse, the fracture surface is perpendicular to the bone, the edges are smooth or finely serrated, without crumbling. There are no fragments, and they fit together closely. On the compression side, there are one or two fracture lines, zigzag, oblique or longitudinal, the surface is at an angle to the bone, the edges are uneven, coarsely serrated, with crumbling, and fragments may be present. The side from which the force acted is established by distinguishing the signs of tension and compression.

In compression, two forces act toward each other. A rail wheel gives a crushed fracture, and a fall from a height gives a compression fracture of a vertebra. Tension is rare and gives an indirect fracture. Twisting, more often in the femur and tibia, forms an indirect spiral fracture. In a direct fracture of a rib, the outer plate shows signs of compression and the inner plate signs of tension. In an indirect fracture it is the reverse, and there is usually no external injury. Attention: in cardiac massage the sternum breaks directly and the ribs indirectly; it is difficult to distinguish this from a blow. Dislocations, however, are always indirect, and external injury is not characteristic.

t: Injuries in falls: fall from a height
n: Types of fall from a height: direct, stepwise and non-free. In an active fall the body gains initial acceleration. The fall is divided into phases: in phases I-II, turning and rotation; in phase III, separation from the support; in phase IV, flight; in phase V, impact with the surface; in phase VI, inertia and secondary impact. Most of the main injuries form in phase V, on impact with the surface; secondary injuries in phase VI. In a fall on the head, the skull and brain are injured; in a fall on the feet, the heel, ankle and shin.

t: Fall onto a plane and requirements for rendering aid
n: A fall onto a plane has three phases: balance is lost, the fall begins, with no injury at this point, and on impact with the surface the main injury forms. In a fall backwards, brain injury is greater on the side opposite the site of impact, that is, in the contrecoup zone. In a fall on the face there is no contrecoup injury. Attention: unlike a fall from a height, in a fall onto a plane there are no secondary injuries and contusion of internal organs is not characteristic. The victim's clothing and footwear are removed without additional damage and handed over to law enforcement within a short time, because they bear traces of the incident.

If the radius of the arc is 0.1 mm or less, the edge of the object is considered a sharp point or a sharp blade. With a sharp object the tissue is first divided, then may be crushed. The injury is always direct. A cutting object gives a spindle-shaped wound, the edges gape, and the length is considerably greater than the depth. The wound from a stabbing object corresponds to the cross-section of the object, oval or slit-like, and internal bleeding is heavier than external. A stabbing-cutting object with one sharp blade gives a "P"-shaped wound, and abrasion at the edges is not characteristic. Attention: one knife, depending on the angle of action, leaves a stab, cut or stab-cut wound.

Chopping objects, that is, axe, adze, sickle and spade, have a sharp blade and a large mass. By a blow they cleave the tissue. Chop injuries are extensive and are often located on the head and arm. Injury to bone and brain and detachment of a body part are possible. According to the circumstances of the incident, chop injuries more often arise in an accident. In homicide and suicide they are very rare. Injuries from sawing objects are rare. They occur in accidents in the household and the timber industry, and sometimes in dismemberment of a corpse.

Let us conclude the topic. Unlike a blunt object, with a sharp object the division of tissue is primary. The injury is always direct. A typical mistake is to confuse cut, stab and chop wounds. The shape of the wound depends on the structure of the object's blade and the direction of action. The victim's clothing should be removed carefully, dried at room temperature and handed to the investigator in paper packaging. Mechanical injuries are divided into those inflicted by blunt objects, by sharp objects and by firearms. The next section may be firearm injuries.
